is_cran_check <- !isTRUE(as.logical(Sys.getenv("NOT_CRAN", "false")))
vignette_artifact <- function(name) {
  path <- system.file(
    "extdata", "vignette-artifacts", name,
    package = "mfrmr",
    mustWork = TRUE
  )
  read.csv(
    path,
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE,
    check.names = FALSE,
    na.strings = character(),
    colClasses = "character"
  )
}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  fig.width = 7,
  fig.height = 5,
  eval = !is_cran_check
)
```

## Choose the result you need

Start with the intended score and decision, then choose a branch. These are
connected workflows, not a checklist requiring every analysis.

| Your situation | Connected route | What to carry into the report |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Define what was rated and whether the design links the groups | `describe_mfrm_data()` → model/design review → `subset_connectivity_report()` or `build_mfrm_network_review()` after fitting | Rubric endpoints, rating unit, assigned/missing rows, shared observations and identification checks. A connected graph alone does not establish a common scale. |
| Estimate person measures and named rater/criterion effects | `fit_mfrm()` → `summary()` → `diagnose_mfrm()` and eligible intervals → `mfrm_results()` → `mfrm_report()` | Model, scale, estimates, uncertainty, Separation/Strata/Reliability, fit and the figures that answer the question. |
| Decide how many raters or tasks a score needs | `mfrm_g_study()` → `mfrm_d_study()` → `plot()` / `summary()` → eligible plan comparisons | [G/D-study](mfrmr-gtheory.html) components, score weights, G/Phi/SEM, future counts and uncertainty. No MFRM fit is required. |
| Describe observed agreement | Match the rating unit → `pairwise_kappa_table()`, `krippendorff_alpha_table()` or `pairwise_icc_table()` | [Agreement](mfrmr-rating-agreement.html) target, category distances/ICC definition, overlap and exclusions. Choose the coefficient from the question. |
| Reuse a scale across forms or waves | Anchor review → anchored fit / linking review → drift and eligible uncertainty | [Anchor provenance and scale](mfrmr-linking-and-dff.html), invariance assumption, fixed versus propagated uncertainty. A common label is not a common calibration. |
| Investigate an unexpected rater/criterion combination or group contrast | Diagnostics → specified `estimate_bias()` or `analyze_dff()` → signed tables and `plot()` → reporting | [Bias/DFF](mfrmr-linking-and-dff.html) target, cell counts, direction, multiplicity and conditional uncertainty; a screen does not establish unfairness. |
| Decide whether another model changes the answer | Matched fits → `compare_mfrm()` → `build_model_choice_review()` → `build_summary_table_bundle()` | [Model comparison](mfrmr-model-choice.html), comparable likelihoods, eligible tests and changes in substantive conclusions. |
| Investigate structure left unexplained or describe groups | Residual diagnostics / `analyze_residual_pca()` / `q3_statistic()` → `mfrm_residual_network()` → `mfrm_report()`; separately, declared entity features → clustering | [Residual exploration](mfrmr-visual-diagnostics.html#residual-networks-ega-and-the-assignment-graph-answer-different-questions) and [feature groups](mfrmr-external-features.html) have different inputs. Retain overlap, feature construction and exploratory status. |
| Give feedback, score new responses or save evidence | Eligible rater report / `score_mfrm_persons()` or portable calibration → plots, export and RDS | Recipient-specific evidence and limitations, scoring prior/calibration version and the source of uncertainty. See the [reporting map](mfrmr-reporting-and-apa.html#choose-report-sections-by-question). |

Before any branch, record the **meaning of low and high scores**. A column
named Comprehensibility may encode ease or difficulty. Higher Person locations
predict higher coded categories; they do not inherently mean better performance.
With the default Rater orientation, higher locations predict lower coded scores.
See [score direction](mfrmr-visual-diagnostics.html#establish-what-higher-scores-mean)
before interpreting severity, bias, plots or anchors. Changing `positive_facets`
is not reverse-coding the outcome.

If Content and Organization are **separate reported scores**, start with the
[criterion-versus-score distinction](mfrmr-gtheory.html#is-a-criterion-a-facet-or-a-score).
A Criterion facet in one-dimensional MFRM does not estimate a separate ability
for each criterion. Multivariate G theory estimates cross-score covariance
components; it does not fit multidimensional IRT.

### Put the network at the stage its edges describe

| Network | Best point in the workflow | What an edge means |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Assignment/co-observation | Design review, before interpreting measures; return to it when planning additional links or anchors | Who shares observed ratings: `mfrm_network_analysis()` → `build_mfrm_network_review()`. Pass `data`, `person`, `facets`, `score` before fitting; use `basis = "planned"` without a score column for an assignment roster. Inspect the person-rater projection as well as the full graph. |
| Rater score relations | After matching shared responses, alongside agreement and rater feedback | Observed score agreement/disagreement or directional differences in `rater_network_analysis()`; cross-criterion observed correlations in `rater_halo_network_analysis()`. These are not residual networks or causal halo tests. |
| Residual associations or communities | After fitting and checking residual/overlap definitions, for a stated unexplained-structure question | Associations left after the model. `mfrm_residual_network()` supplies signed residual correlations and optional hierarchical groups. Report all pairs, overlap and missingness with `mfrm_report()`. This is descriptive exploration, not EGA or a jointly fitted network model. |

An assignment graph is especially useful for explaining why adding a shared
performance or rater might improve linking. It cannot create direct pairwise
agreement evidence where no common responses were rated. Feature clustering
can describe external rater backgrounds; clustering estimated bias or residual
profiles additionally needs explicit aggregation, missingness, comparability
and estimation-uncertainty treatment. The current feature API does not supply
those steps automatically.

## Quick start

By the end of this lesson you should be able to prepare one-rating-per-row
data, estimate abilities and facet effects, identify results needing review,
and save an analysis with its assumptions. Start with the synthetic example,
then adapt the CSV lesson. Follow-up analyses are optional and should answer
your assessment question.

Use this reading route:

| What you need now | Where to go |
| --- | --- |
| Choose a model and estimator for your purpose | [Model and estimator choice](mfrmr-model-choice.html), including when greater complexity helps and when it does not |
| Run and understand a first analysis | Quick start, including individual estimates and review messages below |
| Analyze your own rating sheet | [Use your own CSV](#use-your-own-csv), including stopped checks and wide-to-long reshaping |
| Interpret fit, precision and rater feedback | [Continue with diagnostics and reporting](#continue-with-diagnostics-and-reporting) |
| Find the calculation and its research basis | `help("mfrmr_methods_reference")`, then the linked function's method and References sections |

This tutorial follows the ordinary fixed-facet `fit_mfrm()` workflow. To
plan the number of tasks or raters for an observed score, use
[Plan an assessment with G theory](mfrmr-gtheory.html); no MFRM fit is required
for that workflow. To
choose between fixed facets, shared random raters and Person-specific
testlets, use `mfrmr_output_guide("models")` or
`help("mfrmr_workflow_methods")`. The extended models have dedicated tutorials:
`vignette("mfrmr-random-raters", package = "mfrmr")` and
`vignette("mfrmr-testlets", package = "mfrmr")`. Their prediction targets and
reporting support differ. The diagnostics and reports below follow ordinary
RSM/PCM fits. Two-family GPCM and corrected JML also have class `mfrm_fit`,
but require their model-specific result routes; sharing that class does not
make these ordinary diagnostics available. See `gpcm_capability_matrix()` and
`vignette("mfrmr-gpcm-scope", package = "mfrmr")` before changing model family.

This example estimates person abilities while accounting for rater severity
and criterion difficulty. A *facet* is a source of variation in scores; here,
`Rater` and `Criterion` are facets, and individual raters and criteria are their
*levels*. The data are synthetic, with one row per rating and scores from 1 to 4.

The example data are included in the package. The loading line below creates
`ratings`; you do not need to prepare a file or construct the scores first.
`head(ratings)` shows the first six rows. The quoted column names in `fit_mfrm()`
are case-sensitive; `Study` and `Group` are extra labels unused by this model.
`MML` selects marginal maximum likelihood; `RSM` selects a rating-scale model
with shared category thresholds (the transitions between adjacent scores).
The rubric uses scores 1 through 4. `category_policy = "preserve"` keeps that
category ladder; it prevents an unobserved intermediate category from being
silently collapsed into a different scale.

```{r quick-start, fig.alt = "Wright map of fitted person abilities, rater severities, criterion difficulties and shared category steps for the synthetic ratings. All locations use the same logit scale."}
# Load the package
library(mfrmr)

# Load example ratings and look at the first six rows
ratings <- load_mfrmr_data("example_operational")
head(ratings)

# Fit the model
fit <- fit_mfrm(
  data = ratings,
  person = "Person",
  facets = c("Rater", "Criterion"),
  score = "Score",
  rating_min = 1, rating_max = 4,
  category_policy = "preserve",
  method = "MML",
  model = "RSM"
)

# Plot the results (Wright map)
plot(fit)

# Save the summary, then display its tables
results <- summary(fit)
results$person_overview # One row summarizing person ability estimates
results$facet_overview  # One row per facet: number of levels, mean, SD, range

# Check the interpretation status and recommended next step
results$decision
```

`<-` saves an object without printing it. Here `ratings` holds the data, `fit`
holds the model, and `results` holds its summary. `$` selects a named part:
`results$person_overview` displays just that table. Enter `results` to print
the full summary.

The Wright map displays the estimates in logits, the model's measurement units,
rather than the original 1-to-4 scores. With this example's default orientation,
higher person estimates mean higher ability; higher rater estimates mean
stricter ratings, and higher criterion estimates mean greater difficulty.

The native models use the **logistic metric (L-metric), with D = 1**: there
is no extra 1.7 or 1.702 normal-ogive approximation factor. In this RSM example,
an ability increase of one unit raises each adjacent-category log odds by one,
holding other parameters fixed. For GPCM, the effective discrimination
multiplies that change. A normal ability distribution is a separate assumption
and does not change the response link. See `?fit_mfrm` for scale conventions.

The overview tables describe distributions: `person_overview` has one row for
all 48 persons, and `facet_overview` has one row for each facet. `Mean`/`MeanEstimate`
is the average, `SD`/`SDEstimate` is the spread, and `Min`/`Max` or
`MinEstimate`/`MaxEstimate` give the endpoints. Rater and criterion means are
constrained to zero here; their SDs and ranges show differences among levels.

### Inspect individual estimates

```{r quick-start-estimates}
estimates <- as.data.frame(fit)
head(subset(estimates, Facet == "Person")) # First six persons
subset(estimates, Facet == "Rater")       # All raters
subset(estimates, Facet == "Criterion")   # All criteria
```

`Facet` identifies the type of estimate, `Level` identifies the person, rater,
or criterion, and `Estimate` is its value in logits.

### Check what needs review

Read `results$decision`, especially `Why` and `NextAction`, before interpreting
or reporting estimates. `FormalInference = "No"` in this first summary can
mean that precision has not yet been reviewed; it does not necessarily mean
that fitting failed. The default summary does not compute diagnostics.

```{r quick-start-diagnostics}
diagnostics <- diagnose_mfrm(fit)
diagnostic_summary <- summary(diagnostics)
diagnostic_summary$decision
```

For your own data, follow [Use your own CSV](#use-your-own-csv) below.
For reporting, `res <- mfrm_results(fit, diagnostics = diagnostics)`
builds a comprehensive object that reuses the checks above. Pass `res` to
`mfrm_report()` or `export_mfrm_results()`; `results` remains the basic summary.

## Use your own CSV

The goal here is to estimate person ability while accounting for rater severity
and criterion difficulty in your own ratings. Start with the same row layout
as the packaged example: **one score from one rater for one person on one
criterion**. For example:

| Person | Rater | Criterion | Score |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 001 | R1 | Content | 3 |
| 001 | R1 | Style | 2 |
| 001 | R2 | Content | 4 |
| 001 | R2 | Style | 3 |

The repeated `001` is intentional: all four scores belong to the same person.
Keep IDs consistent across rows. These four rows explain the layout; use the
complete set of ratings for estimation. `Score` contains the ordered integer
categories from the rubric, not totals or averages across raters. This example
uses two non-person facets; choose facets that represent your design.

### 1. Read and inspect the file

You can practice the full workflow without supplying a file. This block writes
the packaged synthetic ratings to a new temporary CSV:

```{r csv-practice-file}
library(mfrmr)
csv_path <- tempfile(fileext = ".csv")
write.csv(load_mfrmr_data("example_operational"), csv_path,
          row.names = FALSE, na = "")
```

For your own data, export your rating sheet as **CSV UTF-8**, with column names
in the first row. Skip the practice block above and select your file instead:

```{r csv-select-file, eval = FALSE}
library(mfrmr)
csv_path <- file.choose()
```

For a reusable script, replace `file.choose()` with a quoted path such as
`"data/ratings.csv"`, relative to the folder shown by `getwd()`.
Both routes now use the same import and analysis code:

```{r csv-read}
ratings <- read.csv(
  csv_path,
  colClasses = "character",
  na.strings = "",
  check.names = FALSE,
  fileEncoding = "UTF-8-BOM"
)
# Treat the documented missing-score marker only in the score column
ratings <- recode_missing_codes(ratings, columns = "Score", codes = "NA")
head(ratings)
names(ratings)
table(ratings$Score, useNA = "ifany")
```

Reading columns as text preserves distinct IDs such as `001`, `1`, and `NA`;
`mfrmr` converts numeric score strings such as `"3"` for estimation.
`check.names = FALSE` preserves the headers. Empty cells are missing in every
column; the literal marker `NA` is recoded only in `Score`. Use the
missing-score markers declared for your data. Zero is a score when the rubric
includes zero, and must not be used to fill unassigned rating cells.

The quoted column names in the next two steps must match `names(ratings)`,
including capitalization and spaces. You do not have to rename your file's
columns. For headers `Student`, `Judge`, `Task`, and `Rating`, change the
arguments in **both** `describe_mfrm_data()` and `fit_mfrm()` as follows:

| Argument | Four-column example | Your alternative headers |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `person` | `"Person"` | `"Student"` |
| `facets` | `c("Rater", "Criterion")` | `c("Judge", "Task")` |
| `score` | `"Score"` | `"Rating"` |

Also use `columns = "Rating"` in the recoding call and inspect `ratings$Rating`
instead of `ratings$Score`. Extra columns such
as the practice file's `Study` and `Group` are unused by this model.

### 2. Review the rows and the rubric

Set the minimum and maximum from the **rubric**, not the observed minimum and
maximum in this sample. The code below describes a 1-to-4 rubric. Keep the same
values in the data review and the fit. `category_policy = "preserve"` preserves the
intended category structure, including categories with no observations.

```{r csv-data-review}
data_review <- describe_mfrm_data(
  data = ratings,
  person = "Person",
  facets = c("Rater", "Criterion"),
  score = "Score",
  rating_min = 1,
  rating_max = 4,
  category_policy = "preserve"
)
data_review$row_retention
data_review$missing_by_column
data_review$score_distribution
data_review$design_connectivity
```

Read these four tables in order:

- `row_retention`: compare input and retained `Rows`; inspect any `DroppedRows`.
  A missing score or required ID removes that rating row, not automatically
  the person's other ratings. The package does not fill missing ratings.
- `missing_by_column`: locate missing input values. Non-numeric score text
  can also cause row loss; inspect warnings and `data_review$preparation_notes`
  when the retained count is unexpected.
- `score_distribution`: `RawN` counts the retained ratings in each category.
  A zero count in an internal category, such as 3 on a 1-to-4 scale, prevents
  fitting with `category_policy = "preserve"`. Review the data and rubric before
  changing categories; increasing optimizer iterations cannot supply missing
  category information.
- `design_connectivity`: `Components = 1` means a facet's levels are connected
  through shared persons. More than one component needs design review before
  comparing levels across components. Connectivity alone does not establish
  full model identification.

For the practice CSV, all 282 input rows are retained, all four categories have
observations, and each facet has one connected component. Six planned ratings
are absent from the file; column missing counts cannot detect absent rows.
If you have a planned assignment roster, pass it as `expected_design` to
`describe_mfrm_data()` to assess these omissions. The applied example later
in this vignette shows how. Without a roster, structural missingness is
reported as not assessed; a complete person-by-rater-by-criterion crossing is
not assumed.

### 3. Fit and read the results

After resolving the data-review findings, fit the same rows, columns, and
rubric. This example uses an RSM with shared category thresholds; the choice
should reflect the scoring design. Diagnostics then supply evidence for the
interpretation decision.

```{r csv-fit}
csv_fit <- fit_mfrm(
  data = ratings,
  person = "Person",
  facets = c("Rater", "Criterion"),
  score = "Score",
  rating_min = 1,
  rating_max = 4,
  category_policy = "preserve",
  method = "MML",
  model = "RSM"
)
csv_diagnostics <- diagnose_mfrm(csv_fit)
csv_results <- summary(csv_fit, diagnostics = csv_diagnostics)
csv_results$decision
```

Read `Why` and `NextAction` before using the estimates. A `FormalInference`
value of `"No"` means that the stated obstacle to formal use still needs
attention. Diagnostic plots can help investigate it. Even a supported precision
decision does not establish the validity of the assessment or answer the
study's substantive question.

```{r csv-results, fig.alt = "Wright map for the ratings read from the example CSV. Compare person, facet and step locations on the fitted scale; the display does not establish that model assumptions hold."}
plot(csv_fit)
csv_estimates <- as.data.frame(csv_fit)
head(subset(csv_estimates, Facet == "Person"))
subset(csv_estimates, Facet == "Rater")
subset(csv_estimates, Facet == "Criterion")
```

`Level` identifies the person, rater, or criterion; `Estimate` is the fitted
value in logits. With these defaults, higher person values mean higher
ability, higher rater values mean stricter ratings, and higher criterion values
mean greater difficulty. The rater and criterion estimates are centered at
zero within each facet. In the practice file, R06 is about +0.41 and R01 about
-0.61: R06 is estimated to rate more strictly after accounting for person
ability and criterion difficulty. This difference alone does not establish
statistical significance.

With custom facet names, change the `Facet` filters too, for example from
`"Rater"` to `"Judge"`; person rows retain `Facet == "Person"` even when the
input ID column is named `Student`. To inspect all persons, remove `head()`.
The overview tables in `csv_results` summarize distributions; the rows in
`csv_estimates` give individual estimates.

### If a check stops you

| What you see | What to check or change |
| --- | --- |
| The CSV is not found | Use `file.choose()` or check the quoted path relative to `getwd()`. An `.xlsx` workbook must first be exported as CSV. |
| All fields appear in one column, or the header is garbled | Check the separator and encoding. Use `sep = ";"` for a semicolon-delimited file; re-export as CSV UTF-8 if text is unreadable. |
| `Column(s) not found in data` | Compare `names(ratings)` with the names in `person`, `facets`, and `score`; check spelling, spaces, and case. |
| Non-numeric or fractional scores | Check `table(ratings$Score, useNA = "ifany")`. Map rubric labels explicitly to their ordered integer codes. Do not round totals or averaged ratings to make them fit. |
| Scores outside the supplied range, such as 99 | Check whether the value is an error or a documented missing code. Correct the value or recode the declared missing marker; keep the range tied to the rubric. |
| Fewer retained rows than expected | Inspect `data_review$missing_by_column` and `data_review$preparation_notes`. Correct unintended missing IDs or score values, then rerun the review and fit. |
| Duplicated person-by-facet cells | Inspect `data_review$duplicate_cell_detail`. Correct accidental duplicates. If these are distinct tasks or occasions, include the corresponding facet; do not automatically delete legitimate ratings. |
| A category has no observations, or the design is disconnected | Review category coding and assignments. Do not invent ratings or change optimizer settings to resolve missing information. |

If your data documentation defines `99` and `.` as missing **scores**, recode
only that column before step 2. This preserves an ID such as `99`:

```{r csv-missing-codes, eval = FALSE}
ratings <- recode_missing_codes(
  ratings, columns = "Score", codes = c("99", ".")
)
table(ratings$Score, useNA = "ifany")
```

Use only the codes declared for your data, and change `"Score"` if your score
column has another name. Then repeat steps 2 and 3 with the recoded data.

### If criteria occupy separate columns

For a sheet with one row per person-rater pair and separate criterion scores,
reshape the criterion columns into rating rows:

```{r csv-wide-to-long}
wide <- data.frame(
  Person = c("001", "001"),
  Rater = c("R1", "R2"),
  Content = c(3, 4),
  Style = c(2, 3)
)
ratings_long <- tidyr::pivot_longer(
  wide,
  cols = c("Content", "Style"),
  names_to = "Criterion",
  values_to = "Score"
)
ratings_long
```

The output is the four-row layout at the start of this section. For your full
sheet, read the CSV into `wide`, select its actual criterion columns in `cols`,
and use `ratings <- ratings_long` before step 2. Keep the complete dataset;
these four demonstration rows are not sufficient for the intended analysis.

## Continue with diagnostics and reporting

The following sections ask three questions: are the estimates interpretable,
what needs closer inspection, and what information belongs in a report?
First select the analysis to carry through every table, figure and export.
The default uses **Quick start**, including its known assignment roster:

```{r reporting-input}
analysis_data <- ratings
fit_toy <- fit
diag_toy <- diagnostics
data("mfrmr_example_operational_design", package = "mfrmr")
analysis_roster <- mfrmr_example_operational_design
```

**For your CSV, run this replacement block instead.** The downstream object
names stay the same so the remaining code uses your analysis:

```{r reporting-csv-input, eval = FALSE}
analysis_data <- ratings
fit_toy <- csv_fit
diag_toy <- csv_diagnostics
analysis_roster <- NULL # Replace with your own planned roster if available
```

Do not use the packaged roster for your own ratings. `NULL` means planned
omissions cannot be assessed; it does not mean there are no missing ratings.
The numerical examples in the prose below describe the synthetic data.
If your headers or rubric differ, update `person`, `facets`, `score`, the
rating limits and later `"Rater"`/`"Criterion"` selections as in the CSV lesson.

### 1. Check the data and estimation record

```{r ratings-setup}
data_review_toy <- describe_mfrm_data(
  data = analysis_data,
  person = "Person",
  facets = c("Rater", "Criterion"),
  score = "Score",
  rating_min = 1,
  rating_max = 4,
  category_policy = "preserve",
  expected_design = analysis_roster
)
data_summary_toy <- summary(data_review_toy)
data_summary_toy$structural_missingness
data_summary_toy$design_connectivity

fit_summary_toy <- summary(fit_toy)
fit_summary_toy$overview[, c("Model", "Method", "N", "Persons", "Converged")]
fit_summary_toy$decision
```

The example has 282 observed ratings from 48 persons, six raters, and three
criteria. All observed rows are retained. Six additional ratings were planned
but are absent; they are visible only because the roster was supplied.
Distinguish omitted planned ratings from input rows excluded during cleaning.
The package does not assume that every rater scored every person.

Record the estimator, model, score coding, constraints, and numerical settings.
For this RSM, MML uses a standard-normal person distribution; reported person
scores are EAP estimates, and non-person facets are fixed effects centered
within facet. RSM shares category thresholds. Choose PCM with an explicit
`step_facet` when the rubric and question call for separate thresholds.

The default MML grid is 31 quadrature points. A comparison that could change
the study's conclusion needs a prespecified denser common-grid sensitivity
check with `mml_quadrature_sensitivity()`. A temporary 7-point grid is only a
computational screening run. `maxit` is a computational ceiling, not a
convergence criterion; inspect `ConvergenceStatus` and `Numerical` before
increasing it. Keep the same data, model, method, and planned controls when
investigating an iteration limit. Choose JML for its fixed-person estimand
when appropriate, not as a faster substitute for MML.

`summary(fit)$numerical_review` distinguishes optimization, curvature, starting
values and integration, with a next action for each. To preserve inputs and
constraints, use `build_mfrm_replay_script(fit)` with the original input data
before changing a diagnostic control. Ordinary `mml_starts` and automatic
integration cannot be combined: review specified starts on a shared fixed grid,
then run `mml_quadrature_sensitivity()` separately. That review retains the
starting-value policy. Nearly equal likelihoods do not override unresolved
gradient, information or inference checks.

```{r ratings-setup-artifacts, echo = FALSE, eval = is_cran_check}
vignette_artifact("workflow_fit_decision.csv")
vignette_artifact("workflow_fit_overview.csv")
```

### 2. Read precision and model fit before interpreting differences

```{r precision-and-fit, fig.alt = "Fitted person, facet and step locations with the requested uncertainty display. Interpret precision using the accompanying table and its stated interval basis."}
diagnostic_summary_toy <- summary(diag_toy)
diagnostic_summary_toy$decision
diagnostic_summary_toy$overall_fit

precision_toy <- precision_review_report(fit_toy, diagnostics = diag_toy)
precision_toy$profile[, c(
  "PrecisionTier", "SupportsFormalInference", "PersonSEBasis", "NonPersonSEBasis"
)]
precision_toy$checks

# View the fitted locations with their uncertainty
plot(fit_toy, diagnostics = diag_toy, show_ci = TRUE)
```

The fit-only summary reports `FormalInference = "No"` until precision evidence
is supplied. Read the diagnostic decision's `Why` and `NextAction` together
with the precision checks. A `model_based` label alone does not override a
failed fit-readiness component or justify a particular substantive claim.

Infit and Outfit describe departures from the fitted response model; their
reference value is 1. A global average near 1 can coexist with local problems.
In this example the MML person uncertainty is posterior SD, while the
non-person SEs use observed information. Report the basis and interval method
when presenting uncertainty; do not call every interval a posterior quantile
interval or treat a point difference as a significance test.

```{r diagnostic-overview-artifact, echo = FALSE, eval = is_cran_check}
vignette_artifact("workflow_diagnostic_overview.csv")
```

### 3. Identify what needs closer inspection

**Are the rating categories working as intended?** Examine category use and
the transitions between scores on the declared rubric:

```{r category-review, fig.alt = "Category-use and threshold summaries for the fitted rubric. Sparse categories and transition ordering should be reviewed together with the rating design."}
scale_toy <- rating_scale_table(fit_toy, diagnostics = diag_toy)
scale_toy$category_table[, c("Category", "Count", "AvgMeasure", "ExpectedMeasure", "Infit", "Outfit")]
scale_toy$model_context
scale_toy$owner_category_table[, c(
  "StepFacet", "CategoryLabel", "RawCount", "Count", "Percent", "UsageStatus"
)]
scale_toy$threshold_table[, c("StepFacet", "Step", "Estimate", "SE", "CIUse")]
plot(scale_toy)
scale_toy$notes
```

`AvgMeasure` is the average oriented generating measure among responses in
each observed category; `ExpectedMeasure` is its model expectation. Category
residual mean squares are descriptive and have no universal unit baseline.

`StepOwner` tells you which facet supplies the thresholds. This RSM has one
`Common` family, so its owner counts describe the whole sample. With PCM,
`step_facet = "Criterion"` gives counts and thresholds for each criterion;
`step_facet = "Rater"` gives them for each rater. Choose the owner from the
rubric and analysis question. Criterion-owned thresholds cannot describe
differences in raters' threshold spread.

`RawCount` counts rating rows; `Count` sums their weights, and `Percent` uses
the total weight within the indicated owner level. These are not counts of
independent persons. A category unused by one owner can be common overall.
`UsageStatus` distinguishes unobserved categories, zero-weight observations
and owners with no ratings; the last have unavailable percentages. An observed
zero does not establish that a category is structurally impossible.

The threshold table reuses SEs and intervals from the supplied diagnostics.
Check `SE_Status`, `CIUse` and `UncertaintySourceStatus` before reporting them.
Without diagnostics, the same call returns counts and fitted threshold points
without requesting covariance calculations; its SEs are unavailable. Notes
remain in the returned object, outside the plot.

The bars show observed category counts; the line shows fitted expected counts.
Look for rarely used categories, changes in average person measure across
categories, and threshold order. Explain the observed pattern in terms of the
rubric. A warning is a reason to investigate, not an automatic instruction to
merge categories.

**Which ratings differ most from model expectations?** This example uses an
explicit exploratory rule and shows up to ten cases:

```{r diagnostics-reporting, fig.alt = "Unusual rating observations selected by the stated residual and probability thresholds. Flags support review of the underlying records, not automatic removal."}
unexpected_toy <- unexpected_response_table(
  fit_toy,
  diagnostics = diag_toy,
  abs_z_min = 1.5,
  prob_max = 0.4,
  top_n = 10
)
unexpected_toy$summary
unexpected_toy$table[, c("Person", "Rater", "Criterion", "Observed", "Expected", "StdResidual")]
plot(unexpected_toy)
```

Read the rule in `$summary` with the residuals. The displayed cases are a
selected preview; `top_n` limits the table, while the summary counts all
flagged ratings. Here this broad rule flags 141 of 282 ratings (50%), although
only ten cases are displayed. Report the rule with the count and percentage.
Inspect the original work and scoring context before changing a
rating or excluding a person. A flag does not identify its cause.

The default diagnostics retain the residual/EAP path and the latent-integrated
marginal screening path. The latter includes category and pairwise agreement
gaps. Keep their bases separate when reporting:

```{r diagnostic-bases, fig.alt = "Marginal fit display based on posterior-averaged response probabilities. Its probability basis differs from conditional residual diagnostics."}
diagnostic_summary_toy$diagnostic_basis[, c("DiagnosticPath", "Status", "ReportingUse")]
plot(fit_toy, type = "marginal_fit", diagnostics = diag_toy)
```

Follow a pairwise warning with `plot()`. Add residual PCA
only when residual structure is relevant to the question, using
`diagnose_mfrm(fit_toy, residual_pca = "both")`. Report the mode and limits of
the screen; residual PCA alone does not establish unidimensionality. See
`vignette("mfrmr-mml-and-marginal-fit", package = "mfrmr")` and
`vignette("mfrmr-visual-diagnostics", package = "mfrmr")` for these follow-ups.

**What should I discuss with a rater?** Start from the coverage and category
checks above, then view severity and its uncertainty alongside the screening
results. Reuse the same fit and diagnostics:

```{r rater-feedback, fig.alt = "Rater severity estimates with 95% normal intervals on the fitted logit scale. Positive estimates indicate stricter ratings relative to the fitted reference."}
plot(fit_toy, type = "rater_severity", diagnostics = diag_toy, facet = "Rater", show_bands = FALSE)
rater_review <- facet_quality_dashboard(
  fit_toy, diagnostics = diag_toy, facet = "Rater"
)
knitr::kable(
  rater_review$detail[, c("Level", "N", "Estimate", "SE", "Infit", "Outfit")],
  digits = 3, row.names = FALSE, caption = "Rater estimates and fit"
)
knitr::kable(
  rater_review$detail[, c("Level", "MissingMetrics", "SeverityFlag", "MisfitFlag")],
  row.names = FALSE, caption = "Availability and screening flags"
)
rater_review$settings
writeLines(strwrap(rater_review$notes, width = 72))
```

A stricter rater is not necessarily inconsistent or incorrect. Individual
interval overlap is not a test of the difference between two raters. Read
`MissingMetrics` before interpreting flags: zero observed flags is not a
complete pass when diagnostics are unavailable. A `REVIEW ONLY` label retains
the fit's restrictions; the plot does not override them.

With the unmodified package defaults (absolute severity at least 1 logit,
Infit or Outfit at or beyond 0.5 and 1.5), none of the six raters is flagged
in this synthetic example. Session options can change the misfit band:
check `rater_review$settings` before comparing your output. A numeric
`misfit_warn = 1.5` instead selects a lower bound of about 0.67; it does not
preserve the default 0.5. These bands prompt review, not a verdict on quality. The earlier response-level screen still
selected 141 ratings: the two screens assess different units and use different
rules. Neither result establishes that every rating is appropriate.

Use the selected unexpected ratings to discuss the rubric and scoring context,
not to automatically exclude a rater. Limited overlap may call for more shared
ratings before comparing raters. A change after training alone does not
establish a training effect. For your own analysis, use `csv_fit` and
`csv_diagnostics`, and replace `"Rater"` with your actual facet name.
Keep the whole dashboard with `saveRDS()` to retain its settings and notes;
`export_mfrm_bundle(..., include = c("dashboard", "html"))` includes them
with the exported tables. See `?facet_quality_dashboard` for that export route.

### 4. Assemble the evidence for a report

```{r primary-route}
res_toy <- mfrm_results(fit_toy, diagnostics = diag_toy, include = "publication")
report_toy <- mfrm_report(res_toy, style = "apa")
report_toy$first_screen[, c("Area", "Status", "MainIssue", "NextAction")]

checklist_toy <- reporting_checklist(fit_toy, diagnostics = diag_toy)
subset(checklist_toy$checklist, !DraftReady,
       c("Section", "Item", "NextAction"))
```

`DraftReady` describes available drafting material with caveats. An unrequested
bias or linking analysis may be irrelevant to the question; do not run every
helper merely to turn every flag `TRUE`. The report's gaps concern the supplied
analysis objects. They cannot confirm recruitment, rater training, ethics,
the study rationale, or whether the prose answers the research question.

For a journal article, the companion
`vignette("mfrmr-reporting-and-apa", package = "mfrmr")` provides a
**Manuscript coverage map**: what to report, where the numerical evidence is,
and what the author must supply. It also shows estimates with uncertainty,
reliability and agreement with distinct interpretations, and a worked
question-to-result explanation.

```{r report-overview-artifact, echo = FALSE, eval = is_cran_check}
vignette_artifact("workflow_next_actions.csv")
```

### 5. Display a table and save the analysis

```{r report-table}
measurements_toy <- fit_measures_table(fit_toy, diagnostics = diag_toy)
rater_table_toy <- subset(
  measurements_toy$table, Facet == "Rater",
  c("Level", "N", "Measure", "SE", "CI_Lower", "CI_Upper", "Infit", "Outfit")
)
apa_table(rater_table_toy, digits = 3,
          caption = "Rater severity and fit",
          note = "N counts rating rows. Rater effects are centered within facet and measured in logits; higher values indicate stricter ratings. Intervals are 95% normal approximations from MML observed-information SEs. Infit and Outfit have reference value 1.")
```

Report the score scale and direction with the table. For person results,
state the EAP/posterior-SD basis; for rater results, explain that variation in
severity is different from inconsistent scoring. Add a sentence answering
the study's question instead of repeating every cell of the table.

```{r report-export}
# A new temporary directory keeps this synthetic example repeatable
export_dir <- tempfile("mfrmr-workflow-export-")
export_toy <- export_mfrm_results(
  res_toy,
  output_dir = export_dir,
  include = c("default", "report"),
  acknowledge_sensitive = TRUE
)
export_preview <- head(export_toy$written_files[, c("Component", "Format", "Path")])
export_preview$Path <- basename(export_preview$Path)
knitr::kable(export_preview, row.names = FALSE,
             caption = "First six exported files (filenames only)")
```

This archive retains the collected results. `acknowledge_sensitive = TRUE` is used
because the example contains synthetic data; it does not remove identifiers
or local paths from real analyses. Review the files before sharing them.
The table previews six filenames; `export_toy$written_files` retains the full
list, and its `Path` column locates the generated files. Temporary
files are for practice; choose a study directory for an archive you will keep.
To reopen the saved analysis without fitting or computing diagnostics, locate
the RDS in that file list:

```{r report-reload}
results_file <- subset(export_toy$written_files, Component == "results_rds")$Path
restored_results <- readRDS(results_file)
summary(restored_results)$decision
```

This restores the collected results and diagnostics. The separate dashboard
object `rater_review` still needs its own `saveRDS()` call as described above.
The exported replay script also reloads the complete RDS; it does not need
`fit` or `diagnostics` from the original session. Run it with
`source("path/to/mfrmr_results_replay.R", chdir = TRUE)`, replacing the path
with the exported script's location. Keep your original data-to-fit script
when you also need to reproduce estimation.
For a fit replay including its input CSV, and for saving a manuscript table,
figure, and their notes, follow Section 5 of
`vignette("mfrmr-reporting-and-apa", package = "mfrmr")`.

```{r export-artifact, echo = FALSE, eval = is_cran_check}
vignette_artifact("workflow_export_files.csv")
```

### Further analyses should answer a stated question

For observed rating agreement, start with the
[rating-agreement tutorial](mfrmr-rating-agreement.html). Its small runnable
example shows how to match person-by-task records, distinguish correlation
from agreement, compare a score source with a reference, and audit missing
pairs without fitting another model. It also explains why these coefficients
answer a different question from rater severity or separation reliability.

For prior sensitivity or an external Bayesian extension, use
`export_mfrm_model()` with a unit-weight RSM/PCM or one-family GPCM MML fit
on the fixed N(0,1) ability scale. Both Stan and brms retain supported fixed
facet anchors and group means. This example reuses the RSM fit above:

```{r model-export-example}
# Reuse the fit above; no additional estimation or backend is needed to export.
stan_model <- export_mfrm_model(
  fit_toy, tempfile("stan-model-"), format = "stan",
  acknowledge_sensitive = TRUE
)
brms_model <- export_mfrm_model(
  fit_toy, tempfile("brms-model-"), format = "brms",
  acknowledge_sensitive = TRUE
)
names(stan_model$files)
model_data <- readRDS(stan_model$files[["model-data.rds"]])
model_data$categories
model_data$priors
```

Each directory contains code, data, category/level mappings and `run.R`.
`stan_model$output_dir` and `brms_model$output_dir` locate these practice
bundles; replace `tempfile()` with a study directory to retain them. The
category table maps the external model's integers back to the original rubric.
`model_data$levels` identifies the Persons and facet levels, and
`model_data$step_owners` identifies the shared RSM or facet-specific PCM steps.
Set `location_prior_sd` and `step_prior_sd` in `export_mfrm_model()` when
creating a bundle for a different prior choice; both formats use those values.
Review its README and priors, then run the script from that directory with
CmdStanR/CmdStan installed (and brms for the second format). Export itself
needs neither backend. Both formats preserve adjacent-category probabilities,
the fixed standard-normal ability scale, facet signs and constraints, and
unordered step offsets with their original sum constraints. Their explicit structural priors make this
a Bayesian analysis; it does not reproduce MML point estimates or qualify
frequentist interval coverage. Two-family GMFRM also supports Stan export,
with explicit component log-slope priors and a `slope-levels.csv` mapping; see
the [two-family workflow](mfrmr-gpcm-scope.html). One-family GPCM uses
`log_slope_prior_sd` in both formats, with geometric-mean-one slopes. For brms,
the source must use `gpcm_mml_identification = "fixed_standard_normal"`.
The default one-family GPCM estimates the population mean and variance.
You can export its intercept-only population to Stan with
`population_prior = list(mean = c(0, 1), log_sd = c(0, 0.5))`; each pair gives
the location and scale of a normal prior. The mean and SD are sampled while
relative slopes and anchors retain the native metric. brms still requires the
fixed-population specification. Changing that setting changes the model; do not
change it merely to enable export. Review prior predictions and sensitivity.

Anchor values are exact constraints. `levels.csv` and `steps.csv` in anchored
or one-family bundles show the prior means, marginal SDs and fixed coordinates.
A zero SD reflects a fixed value, not evidence that its earlier calibration
was certain. The scope excludes JML/Person anchors, two-family brms,
nonunit weights, population regression, interactions and shrinkage. Native
two-family fitting still excludes anchors. Inspect
sampler diagnostics and prior sensitivity before using the posterior. Exported
ratings and original labels require the same sharing review as an analysis
archive. See `?export_mfrm_model` for supported post-processing and prediction
targets.

After sampling, start with `summary-decision.csv`: it states the sampling
review and next action before presenting estimates. `sampling-review.csv`
lists the checks and criteria. `parameter-summary.csv` keeps original labels,
the meaning of larger values, fixed/estimated status and interval status
beside the numbers. Fixed values have no estimated interval; finite intervals
for estimated values can still require sampling review. Both formats support
`Rscript run.R --summarize` to rebuild these reports from saved draws without
sampling again. A clean sampling screen does not establish model validity.

Bring those summaries back into mfrmr with `read_mfrm_posterior()`. This small
included example has short chains and intentionally retains a sampling-review
status. It demonstrates the reporting path without fitting or requiring Stan.

```{r saved-posterior-return}
posterior <- read_mfrm_posterior(system.file(
  "extdata", "posterior-example", package = "mfrmr"))
summary(posterior)
posterior_plot <- plot(posterior, quantity = "location", draw = FALSE)
posterior_report <- mfrm_report(posterior, style = "apa")
```

For your analysis, supply the export directory instead. Use
`as_ggplot(posterior_plot)` for an editable figure,
`plot_data(posterior_plot, "table")` for its long table, and
`mfrm_report(posterior, output = "html")` for the full report. `confint(posterior)`
retrieves saved 95% **credible** intervals, keeping fixed values and review
flags. Other levels, contrasts, predictions and density/raincloud plots need
the backend's joint draws; they cannot be recovered from this summary.

| Question | Follow-up |
| --- | --- |
| How uncertain is a specified difference between two raters? | `mfrm_facet_intervals()` uses their covariance; choose the model-based or sandwich method for the sampling assumptions. Attach the result with `mfrm_results(fit, intervals = ...)`. See `mfrmr-facet-intervals`; an ordinary Wright map does not switch to sandwich intervals. |
| Do category thresholds need to differ by criterion? | `compare_mfrm()` and `mml_quadrature_sensitivity()`; fit candidates to the same observations and review numerical sensitivity. |
| Which facet combinations merit closer review? | `estimate_all_bias(fit)` explores all non-Person pairs. `summary(screens)$overview` shows availability and magnitude; `$cells` preserves signed shifts and counts. Use `plot(screens)` and `plot(screens, pair = "Rater x Criterion")` for overview and detail. These conditional screens have no collection-wide multiplicity control. |
| Do prespecified rater-by-criterion or group contrasts depart from the model? | `estimate_bias()` supplies conditional screening evidence; `analyze_dff()` has its own scope. For jointly fitted interactions, see `fit_mfrm(facet_interactions = ...)` and `interaction_effect_table()`. Specify the target, supported inference route and multiplicity plan before inspecting results. See the reporting vignette and `mfrmr-linking-and-dff`. |
| How often does a declared rater-warning rule detect a specified departure or falsely flag an unaffected rater? | `mfrm_screening_performance()` with known simulation truth and all planned trials. See `mfrmr-screening-performance` for individual/family rates, unavailable results and Monte Carlo uncertainty. |
| Would the conclusions change under a GPCM? | `gpcm_capability_matrix()` and `mfrmr-gpcm-scope`; explain what discrimination reweighting means for the score interpretation. |
| Are scores missing from assigned rating events? | Start with the assignment roster, then `review_mfrm_imputations()`, `fit_mfrm_imputed()` and `pool_mfrm_imputed()`. See `mfrmr-response-imputation` for an explicit imputation model; the review function does not generate scores. Do not fill unassigned combinations. |
| Do external attributes describe different groups of persons, raters or tasks? | `mfrm_features()` with PCA/k-means for numeric features, or PAM/hierarchical clustering for mixed features. See `mfrmr-external-features` for missing attributes, group stability and links back to rating events. Groups are not ability classes or judgments of rater quality. |
| Would more raters or tasks improve observed-score dependability? | `mfrm_g_study()` followed by `mfrm_d_study()`; declare the observed-score design, candidate plans and any composite weights. Their help explains G/Phi and SEM. These coefficients describe observed scores, not MFRM latent abilities. |
| Are forms or waves on a comparable scale? | `mfrmr-linking-and-dff` and `mfrmr-portable-calibration`; common labels alone do not establish linking. |
| How does a proposed rating design perform under stated assumptions? | `build_mfrm_sim_spec()`, `simulate_mfrm_recovery()`, and `assess_mfrm_recovery()`; report generating conditions, repetitions, failures, and Monte Carlo uncertainty. |
| How should new persons be scored under an existing calibration? | `predict_mfrm_units()` and `sample_mfrm_plausible_values()`; reuse an eligible fitted calibration and report the conditioning assumptions. |
| How certain is a person's placement relative to supplied ability cuts? | For ordinary RSM/PCM, use `cut_scores` in the eligible scoring API and inspect `$decisions`. `apa_table(..., which = "decisions")` retains probabilities, priors and review states. Check whether the scoring prior represents the target population; numerical checks do not establish that match. See `mfrmr-portable-calibration` for interpretation and saved-score reporting; calibration and estimated-prior uncertainty are excluded. |

For repeated simulation work, supply `file` to `simulate_mfrm_recovery()` or
`evaluate_mfrm_design()`. An identical call reads a finished result or resumes
saved trials after interruption. For example, create a results directory once
and keep this call in the analysis script:

```{r simulation-file-workflow, eval=FALSE}
dir.create("results", showWarnings = FALSE)
recovery <- simulate_mfrm_recovery(
  n_person = 50, n_rater = 4, n_criterion = 4,
  reps = 100, seed = 20261021, file = "results/recovery.rds"
)
summary(recovery)$rep_overview  # Retains failed attempts, too.
```

The default `file_refit = "never"` rejects a file whose inputs, fitting controls,
replication count, RNG kind or implementation/software identity differ. Use a
new path to preserve both studies, or explicitly choose `"on_change"` to replace
an incompatible study. `"always"` starts again even if the file matches.
After completion, ordinary `readRDS()` also loads the result and its
`reproducibility` metadata. Save the script and software environment with it;
seed recording is not a guarantee of identical numerical results on every
platform. See `?simulate_mfrm_recovery` for checkpoint boundaries and parallel
resumption.

For an injected Group-by-Criterion or Rater-by-Criterion departure,
`evaluate_mfrm_signal_detection()` summarizes the behavior of the selected
screen. Start with `summary(x)$detection_summary`: compare the planned and
available counts before interpreting a rate. Non-target rates average the
available-cell proportion within each contributing trial; they are neither
pooled-cell rates nor the probability of any false flag. Inspect
`x$rep_overview` for failed stages and seeds, and `x$results` for target-level
unavailability reasons. This helper uses `saveRDS()` for saving the returned
result, without the checkpoint arguments shown above.

DIF contrasts are reference minus focal. A residual-score difference is not
the injected latent effect; a subgroup location difference requires common-scale
linking before its mean is reported. The bias shift is relative to the fitted
baseline. These summaries do not establish effect recovery or calibrated
power. Residual DIF tests remain unavailable, and refit/bias rates remain
screening summaries. See `?evaluate_mfrm_signal_detection` for denominators,
Monte Carlo uncertainty and interpretation of older saved results.

When starting from `extract_mfrm_sim_spec(fit)`, inspect the proposed generating
mechanism. Without a population regression, the Person spread is the SD of the
reported estimates; shrinkage and measurement error mean it need not equal the
latent population SD. With a population regression, the stored coefficients,
residual variance, transformations and factor coding define Person generation.
The generating parameters remain fixed across replications. Monte Carlo SEs
measure the precision of the simulation averages under those assumptions;
they do not measure uncertainty in the original fit or validate future forecasts.
When covariates and observed assignments belong to the same template Persons,
use `population_assignment = "matched"` (the default for newly built/extracted
specifications). Matching `TemplatePerson` IDs preserve the association between
covariates, groups and assignment patterns. Choose `"independent"` only when
breaking that association is part of the intended scenario. A population
`Group` column also defines the response group; conflicting group definitions
are rejected. Truth metadata retain the selected source template IDs.

Observed skeletons preserve repeated rows and weights. Each row generates a
new conditionally independent rating; dependence across occasions or among
peer reviewers requires a different generating model. Remove accidental source
duplicates before building the specification. Weights affect fitting and do
not create extra generated responses. Older saved specifications without
`population_assignment` keep independent template draws; rebuild them and use
a new study file for matched sampling.

For a manual refit of generated latent-regression data, take both `person_data`
and `population_formula` from `attr(simulated_data, "mfrm_population_data")`.
The formula-compatible terms object retains the template's transformation basis
and factor coding. Rewriting it as a fresh `~ scale(X)` formula would relearn
the scaling on the new cohort. Old transformed specifications without the stored
basis must be rebuilt from the original template or fit and saved as a new study.

Read recovery results as relative parameter recovery under the declared
generating conditions. `summary(recovery)$recovery_summary` reports RMSE and
its Monte Carlo SE across independent trials. Mean-aligned group bias is zero
by construction, so a small value does not establish unbiased estimation of
each parameter. PCM/GPCM comparisons account for the facet shift induced by
centering the generating step thresholds.

For interval evidence, read `Coverage95` together with `ExpectedRows`,
`CoverageRows`, `CoverageAvailabilityRate`, `McseCoverage95` and `FailedReps`.
Coverage is conditional on obtaining a valid interval; failures and unavailable
intervals remain visible separately. Non-Person MML facet coverage uses each
level's deviation from its facet mean with the matching covariance. JML point
recovery and Person scores remain useful, but their source uncertainty is not
treated as that structural interval; inspect `CIReason` in `recovery$recovery`
or `CIReasons` in the summary. Unknown target rosters produce `NA` rates, not
zero or successful outcomes. `assess_mfrm_recovery(recovery)$uncertainty_review`
keeps these counts and reasons with its checklist.

For older saved objects, `summary()`, assessment and summary/coverage plotting
recalculate the aggregates without fitting. They withhold legacy coverage
when the required covariance was not saved. A new run is needed for corrected
PCM/population truth mapping and matching interval evidence; retain the old
file as a separate study. The help page explains which fields can be recovered.

For stability against an observed-data reference, use
`build_mfrm_resampling_spec()` and `draw_mfrm_resamples()`. They resample entire
Person clusters within optional strata, retaining all ratings for each selected
Person. A same-size bootstrap requires `design = "stratified_bootstrap"`,
`sample_fraction = 1`, and `topup_preserve_facets = FALSE`; the default fraction
is one half. Adding Persons to restore missing facet levels changes the
sampling distribution. Read `sampling_scheme` and the base/added/final counts
in the manifests. Person resampling holds the observed non-Person facets fixed;
it does not reproduce sampling new raters/tasks or dependence among Persons
in a peer-review network. Full-data estimates are uncertain references, not
known truth, and these helpers do not qualify bootstrap confidence intervals.

Missing **attributes** and missing **rating scores** need different models and
workflows. Neither clustering nor response-score imputation is a prerequisite
for ordinary MFRM analysis. G/D-studies start from observed scores and their
design; do not substitute MFRM estimates or testlet variances for their input.
For these branches, `mfrmr_output_guide("features")`,
`mfrmr_output_guide("imputation")` and `mfrmr_output_guide("gtheory")` identify
the supported summaries and plots. Save their full objects with `saveRDS()`;
they have dedicated output routes and are not `mfrm_results()` inputs.

Simulation examples with one or two repetitions test the computational setup;
they do not estimate operating characteristics adequately for a paper. A
simulation's assumptions and results also do not replace evidence from the
observed assessment. Keep these analyses in the report only when their role
in answering the study question is clear.

## An observed writing-assessment example

The optional `sirt` package supplies `data.ratings1`, observed German-writing
ratings from a 2009 Austrian educational standards survey. Its 274 rows contain
135 students, seven observed raters and five rubric criteria scored 0 to 3.
The [data documentation](https://alexanderrobitzsch.r-universe.dev/sirt/doc/manual.html#data.ratings)
describes the source. This dataset is separate from mfrmr's synthetic examples.

The practical question is which differences in severity, category use or
consistency merit discussion with a rater. The example below uses a PCM so
criteria can have different category thresholds. It assumes a common writing
scale and conditionally independent ratings; inspecting the output does not
establish those assumptions. Repeated rubric ratings of one performance may
still share influences that this model does not represent.

Run this optional example after installing `sirt`. It is not run when building
this vignette. Display aliases replace source identifiers in the example's
tables; aliases do not make a rating archive anonymous.

```{r observed-writing-example, eval = FALSE}
library(mfrmr)
data("data.ratings1", package = "sirt")
wide <- data.ratings1
persons <- match(wide$idstud, unique(wide$idstud))
raters <- match(wide$rater, unique(wide$rater))
writing <- do.call(rbind, lapply(paste0("k", 1:5), function(criterion) {
  data.frame(
    Person = sprintf("P%03d", persons), Rater = paste0("R", raters),
    Criterion = criterion, Score = wide[[criterion]]
  )
}))
review <- describe_mfrm_data(
  writing, person = "Person", facets = c("Rater", "Criterion"), score = "Score",
  rating_min = 0, rating_max = 3
)
review$row_retention
review$design_connectivity

writing_fit <- fit_mfrm(
  writing, "Person", c("Rater", "Criterion"), "Score",
  method = "MML", model = "PCM", step_facet = "Criterion",
  rating_min = 0, rating_max = 3, quad_points = 61, maxit = 400
)
writing_diagnostics <- diagnose_mfrm(writing_fit, residual_pca = "none")
feedback <- facet_quality_dashboard(
  writing_fit, diagnostics = writing_diagnostics, facet = "Rater"
)
feedback$detail[, c("Level", "N", "Estimate", "SE", "Infit", "Outfit", "MisfitFlag")]
feedback$settings
plot(writing_fit, type = "rater_severity", diagnostics = writing_diagnostics, facet = "Rater", show_bands = FALSE)
saveRDS(feedback, "writing-feedback.rds")
archive <- export_mfrm_bundle(
  writing_fit, diagnostics = writing_diagnostics, facet = "Rater",
  output_dir = "writing-analysis", data = writing, acknowledge_sensitive = TRUE
)
```

Reshaping gives 1,370 criterion ratings; the 274 original rows are not the
number of students. Each rater has 185 to 205 criterion ratings here. The
example produces a low-Infit flag for R7: unusually predictable ratings also
trigger this screen. This is a prompt to inspect rubric use and individual
ratings, not evidence that R7 is inaccurate or should be removed. Severity
and consistency answer different questions, and this dataset supplies no
known true rater quality against which to validate either interpretation.

The quadrature setting belongs to this example; use
`mml_quadrature_sensitivity()` when numerical sensitivity matters to a
comparison. Preserve the dashboard's notes, review rating-category use and
common-person coverage, and use the actual scripts or rubric descriptors in
feedback discussions. A different-looking result alone does not establish
that a rater needs training or that training would improve the scores.
